title: Action! Action Now.
body_text: So I wrote the other day about the severe damage the Trump administration has done to US federally funded science, and mentioned the even more severe damage they are planning. This is contained in an irritatingly lengthy and gassy Office of Management and Budget proposal, which boils down to some key horrible ideas (summarized, for example, by Elizabeth Ginexi here) and at BioCentury here (free link). Section 200.205 will require that political appointees (and not professional staffers at any granting agency, scientific review boards, etc.) will be in charge of awards. The political appointees will be required to sign off on every grant before it is awarded, and they are forbidden to defer to peer review recommendations. They are explicitly charged with looking for anything that touches on illegal immigration, non-binary sexual definitions, anything that smacks of diversity-equity-inclusion, or indeed anything at all that is deemed to promote “anti-American” values. That last category, naturally, is up to the discretion of the overseers. Oh yeah, awards must also “demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities”. Funds cannot be used for any messaging that, in the opinion of the agency heads, promotes or opposes any policies unrelated to the exact objectives of the award. All this alone is enough of a blueprint for disaster, obviously. But that same section goes on to pound the nails in further by emphasizing that peer review recommendations must not be considered as binding in any way on the decisions of the political staff, and that all grants must comply with the administration’s “Gold Standard Science” ideas. Institutions that have shown themselves willing to get on board with this nebulous cloud of bullshit will get priority in grant awards; it says so in as many words (well, minus the “nebulous bullshit” part). What is “Gold Standard Science”, you may well ask? Whatever the administration likes. No definitions are provided. What’s more, active grants will be subject to termination at any time if they are held to be inconsistent with agency priorities. Who decides that? Why, political appointees, who else?. No other basis is needed - no accusations of proof of malfeasance or fraud, just “We don’t like it”. As mentioned in the last post, there are also broad prohibitions against any use of federal funds for collaboration with a whole list of countries, starting with China. Any use at all - paper publication charges, travel, reagents, doesn’t matter. And in fact any international aspect at all to any grant (whether it involves “listed” countries or others) would have to be signed off on by agency overseers. The straps are tightened in every way you can imagine: grant awardees can be disqualified on the basis of any affiliation with any organization that the US government deems to “undermine public safety”. All conference attendance, anywhere, must first be approved at an agency level - and if you take the language literally, it must be spelled out in the initial grant application to be considered a valid request. The same goes for use of funds for any memberships in any professional societies. Use of such funds for journal subscriptions is just disallowed from the start, as are uses of funds for all publication charges and open-access fees. Any uses of grant funds for any costs for public outreach are explicitly barred. There’s more - see the link above for the details. But this should be more than enough to show what this administration wants to do and how they want to do it. Everything has to be explicitly aligned with Trump priorities, and any deviations will immediately be punished at both a personal and institutional level. Alles klar, Herr Kommisar? So what’s to be done about all this? First, an easy one. Like all such Federal regulations, this one has an Open Comment period, and these comments can be made at this link. There is a blue “Comment” button in the upper left part of the page. As I write, there are another 41 days left. At the moment, there are 3,232 comments, 1,932 of which have been made today, and I just left what must be number one thousand, nine hundred and thirty-three, unless someone beat me to it while I was typing. So that’s a start. There will be court challenges to all this stuff, but given the tenor of Supreme Court decisions these last few months, I would not want to depend on the judiciary to save us. So we need to pressure scientific societies and industry to add their voices to this. The AAAS is already speaking out, to its credit - see this editorial by Holden Thorp here at Science. But let’s not stop there! Hey, American Chemical Society! You’ve been very, very quiet overall (although perhaps that’s getting better) but this is the time to get loud. Does the ACS have any thoughts at all on these proposed changes to the way that academic science is funded in this country? How about the other scientific societies like the ASM? ASCO? The American Heart Association? The Society for Neuroscience? We can keep going. If you don’t make your voices known now, what exactly are you waiting for? And how about the very industry where I have been working all these years? You have influence and you damn well know it. There are the trade groups like PhRMA and BIO, but let’s not wait on them to hash out statements. Every CEO should, in a better world, be saying something - because this is actually a severe threat to the entire business, as all of you realize very well if you let yourselves think about it. Steve Usdin at BioCentury has the right idea here: The leaders of the industry’s largest companies understand exactly what is at stake. They understand the consequences of replacing peer review with political review. They understand the damage that would result if universities lose funding because of ideology rather than scientific performance. And they understand that once the foundations of the system are dismantled, rebuilding them could take decades. They will be judged not by what they understood, but by what they did. Damn right. Speak up! Now’s the time! Standing by the side of the room, glancing around nervously and hoping that somebody else does something will lead us to disaster. These are not normal times, so stop acting as if they are.
